lead: This unit explains why classical physics fails for small objects and how quantum mechanics replaces it. You will use photons, matter waves, the uncertainty principle and the Schrodinger equation to find allowed energies and probabilities. After it you can solve a particle in a box, read a wavefunction correctly, and estimate tunnelling probabilities.
about: This unit follows the road from the failure of classical physics to the working rules of quantum mechanics. Chapter 6.1 starts with black-body radiation and Planck's energy quantum. Chapter 6.2 uses photons to explain the photoelectric and Compton effects. Chapter 6.3 states wave-particle duality and the de Broglie relation, and 6.4 tests matter waves in the Davisson-Germer experiment and separates group and phase velocity. Chapter 6.5 introduces the uncertainty principle, which forces a probability description. Chapters 6.6 and 6.7 develop the wavefunction, its Born interpretation, and the time-dependent and time-independent Schrodinger equations. Chapter 6.8 solves the particle in a one- and three-dimensional box, and 6.9 applies the same ideas to barrier penetration and tunnelling.

chapters.idea: A hot body's spectrum forced Planck to say that energy is emitted in discrete quanta E = hν, not continuously.
chapters.depth: Start with a black body as a small hole in a hot cavity. Show the experimental spectrum: intensity per wavelength against λ, peak moving to shorter λ as T rises. Give Wien's displacement law λmax T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K and the Rayleigh-Jeans law, then the ultraviolet catastrophe. Planck's fix: oscillators emit energy in quanta E = hν, with h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. Some syllabi call this cavity radiation or early radiation theory. Keep derivation of the full Planck curve short; exam asks the idea and the graph.

figure.title: From black-body curve to Planck quanta
figure.aria: A downward flow from a hot body to the classical Rayleigh-Jeans law, its ultraviolet catastrophe at short wavelength, Planck's energy quanta, and the matched black-body spectrum.

chapters.example: A black body at 6000 K peaks at wavelength λmax. Use Wien's law λmax T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K to find λmax. Then find the photon energy hν at that peak. Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Answer: λmax = 4.83 × 10⁻⁷ m = 483 nm; ν = 6.21 × 10¹⁴ Hz; E = 4.11 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 2.57 eV.
chapters.trap: Treating Planck's E = hν as continuous classical energy, or using Wien's law as if it gave total intensity. Wien gives only the peak wavelength.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3: electromagnetic waves and black-body ideas; Unit 2: wave graphs; basic calculus.
chapters.leave: Full derivation of Planck's law from cavity modes and Bose-Einstein statistics; Stefan-Boltzmann law derivation.

chapters.idea: Light delivers energy in photon packets: one photon ejects one electron in the photoelectric effect, and one X-ray photon shares energy and momentum in Compton scattering.
chapters.depth: Photoelectric effect: threshold frequency ν0, work function φ = hν0, stopping potential eV0 = hν − φ, and Kmax independent of intensity. Use the Kmax against ν graph; slope is h. Compton effect: X-ray photon scatters from a free electron, λ′ − λ = (h/mec)(1 − cos θ), Compton wavelength 2.43 pm. Include recoil electron and conservation of energy-momentum. Some syllabi call this Compton scattering. Keep the four-vector derivation out; use the formula and one angle.

figure.title: Two photon interactions
figure.aria: A photon branches into a photoelectric path that emits an electron and a Compton path that gives a scattered photon and a recoil electron.

chapters.example: Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal with work function 2.0 eV. Find the stopping potential. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Answer: photon energy = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.10 eV; Kmax = 1.10 eV; stopping potential = 1.10 V.
chapters.trap: Mixing intensity with photon energy: brighter light gives more electrons, not larger Kmax. Stopping potential depends on frequency and work function, not intensity.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 Planck quanta; Unit 3: EM waves; Unit 4: wave picture of light.
chapters.leave: Full Compton derivation with four-momentum; photoelectric effect in solids and band details, left to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Every moving particle has a matter wave with de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p, so wave and particle descriptions are two faces of one object.
chapters.depth: Wave-particle duality: light shows photon behaviour, electrons show diffraction. de Broglie relation λ = h/p, with p momentum. For an electron accelerated through V volts, λ = 12.27/√V Å. Define matter waves and the meaning of λ for a cricket ball versus an electron. Include the electron double-slit idea qualitatively. Some syllabi call this wave properties of particles. Use the nonrelativistic formula at low energy; do not derive relativistic corrections unless energy is high.

figure.aria: A Venn diagram of wave properties and particle properties; the overlap holds de Broglie's relation λ = h/p.

chapters.example: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Answer: λ = h/√(2meV) = 1.227 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 0.123 nm.
chapters.trap: Using λ = h/p with the wrong p. At low voltage use p = √(2meV); at energies comparable to 511 keV use relativistic momentum.
chapters.prereq: 6.2 photon momentum; Unit 2: wave ideas; Unit 1: relativistic momentum for high energies.
chapters.leave: Electron diffraction in crystals beyond Davisson-Germer; full relativistic quantum theory.

chapters.idea: The Davisson-Germer experiment confirms matter waves by electron diffraction, while group velocity is the speed of the particle and phase velocity is not.
chapters.depth: Davisson-Germer experiment: 54 eV electrons on nickel, detector peak at 50°, Bragg condition nλ = 2d sin θ confirms λ = h/p. Some texts spell it Davison-Germer. Then group velocity vg = dω/dk and phase velocity vp = ω/k. For matter waves vg equals particle speed; nonrelativistically vp = v/2, relativistically vp = c²/v. Show why a wave packet moves at vg. Keep crystal-plane geometry simple.

figure.title: Davisson-Germer test
figure.aria: An electron gun sends 54 eV electrons to a nickel crystal, a detector at 50 degrees finds a first-order diffraction peak, and a Bragg check gives wavelength 1.67 angstrom.

chapters.example: 54 eV electrons strike a nickel crystal and give a first-order diffraction peak at 50°. Find the de Broglie wavelength. Using d = 2.03 Å, find the Bragg angle θ in nλ = 2d sin θ and compare 2θ with 50°. Answer: λ = 1.67 Å; sin θ = 0.411; θ = 24.3°; 2θ = 48.6°, close to 50°.
chapters.trap: Confusing phase velocity with group velocity for matter waves. Nonrelativistically vp = v/2, while vg equals the particle speed v.
chapters.prereq: 6.3 de Broglie relation; Unit 2: wave velocity; Unit 4: diffraction and Bragg reflection.
chapters.leave: Detailed crystal structure, reciprocal lattice and Brillouin zones; band theory is in Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Position and momentum cannot both be sharp: Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2, and similar limits apply to energy and time.
chapters.depth: State Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2 and ΔE Δt ≥ ℏ/2. Explain from single-slit diffraction: narrow slit gives small Δx and broad pattern, so large Δp. Use it to show no sharp trajectory. Apply to natural linewidth, zero-point energy and minimum kinetic energy in a trap. Some syllabi call it Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. Keep the gamma-ray microscope qualitative; exam usually asks the statement, meaning and one estimate.

figure.title: Uncertainty from a slit
figure.aria: An electron wave passes a narrow slit, spreads by diffraction, and sets the uncertainty product at least h-bar over two.

chapters.example: An electron is confined to a region of size Δx = 0.1 nm. Estimate the minimum momentum uncertainty and the kinetic energy from Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2. Use ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Answer: Δp ≥ 5.28 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s; K ≈ (Δp)²/(2m) = 1.53 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 0.95 eV.
chapters.trap: Treating Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2 as an exact equality. It is a lower bound, and the estimate uses an order-of-magnitude Δp.
chapters.prereq: 6.3 matter waves; 6.4 wave packet; Unit 2: diffraction.
chapters.leave: Full gamma-ray microscope derivation and commutator algebra; advanced operator methods.

chapters.idea: The wavefunction ψ is a complex amplitude, and |ψ|² gives the probability density of finding the particle.
chapters.depth: Wavefunction ψ(x,t) is complex and carries all available information. Born rule: probability in dV is |ψ|² dV; probability density is |ψ|² = ψ*ψ. Normalization ∫|ψ|² dV = 1. Conditions: finite, single-valued, continuous, and continuous derivative where V is finite. Mention expectation value ⟨A⟩ = ∫ψ* Â ψ dV. Some syllabi call this properties and significance of the wave function. Keep operator algebra minimal.

figure.aria: A bell-shaped wavefunction and its narrower probability density, both centred at zero, with the probability density never negative.

chapters.example: A wavefunction is ψ(x) = A e^(−x²/(2a²)) on the x-axis, with a = 1.0 nm. Find A from normalization ∫|ψ|² dx = 1. Use ∫ e^(−x²/a²) dx = a√π. Answer: A² a√π = 1, so A = 1/√(a√π) = 2.37 × 10⁴ m^(−1/2).
chapters.trap: Forgetting normalization and treating ψ itself as probability. Probability density is |ψ|², and ψ may be complex.
chapters.prereq: 6.5 uncertainty; Unit 2: wave equation; complex numbers and Gaussian integrals.
chapters.leave: Hilbert-space formalism, Dirac notation and probability current; advanced quantum courses.

chapters.idea: The Schrodinger equation is the wave equation of matter; when V does not depend on time, it splits into stationary states with definite energy.
chapters.depth: Time-dependent Schrodinger equation iℏ ∂ψ/∂t = −(ℏ²/2m)∇²ψ + Vψ. For V independent of time, separate ψ = ψ(x)φ(t) to get the time-independent equation −(ℏ²/2m)∇²ψ + Vψ = Eψ. Explain stationary states, eigenfunctions, eigenvalues and boundary conditions. Solve the free particle as a plane wave and connect k, ω and E. Some syllabi call the time-independent form the steady-state equation. Keep the harmonic oscillator out.

figure.title: From TDSE to steady state
figure.aria: The time-dependent Schrodinger equation separates when potential is time-independent, giving the time-independent equation and energy eigenvalues for stationary states.

chapters.example: For a free electron with wave number k = 1.0 × 10¹⁰ m⁻¹, use the time-independent Schrodinger equation with V = 0 to find E and angular frequency ω. Use ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Answer: E = ℏ²k²/(2m) = 6.11 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.81 eV; ω = E/ℏ = 5.79 × 10¹⁵ rad/s.
chapters.trap: Using the time-independent equation when V depends on time, or dropping boundary conditions. Stationary states need V independent of t.
chapters.prereq: 6.6 wavefunction; partial derivatives; Unit 3: wave equation.
chapters.leave: Solving the harmonic oscillator and hydrogen atom; advanced separation methods.

chapters.idea: Confining a particle in an infinite box quantises its energy, and the same boundary conditions extend to three dimensions.
chapters.depth: One-dimensional infinite well: V = 0 inside 0 < x < L, infinite outside. Boundary conditions ψ(0) = ψ(L) = 0 give ψn = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L), En = n²h²/(8mL²), n = 1,2,3... Show nodes and spacing. Three-dimensional box: Enx,ny,nz = (h²/8m)(nx²/Lx² + ny²/Ly² + nz²/Lz²); for a cube states with the same n² sum are degenerate. Mention finite well only through exponential tails; full finite-well solution is not required here.

figure.aria: The first three normalized wavefunctions of an infinite square well, with n minus one nodes inside the box.

chapters.example: An electron is in a one-dimensional infinite box of width L = 1.0 nm. Find the first three energies in eV. Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Answer: E1 = 0.376 eV, E2 = 1.50 eV, E3 = 3.38 eV.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that n starts at 1 for an infinite well; n = 0 gives ψ = 0. Also check whether L is the full box width.
chapters.prereq: 6.7 time-independent Schrodinger equation; boundary conditions; trigonometry.
chapters.leave: Full finite-well solution and degeneracy breaking; only qualitative tails are used in 6.9.

chapters.idea: A particle can pass through a barrier even when E < V, with probability falling exponentially with barrier width.
chapters.depth: Rectangular barrier of height V and width a for E < V. Inside, the wavefunction decays as e^(−κx), κ = √(2m(V−E))/ℏ. For a thick barrier, transmission T ≈ e^(−2κa). Explain classically forbidden but quantum allowed. Applications: alpha decay, tunnel diode, scanning tunnelling microscope, nuclear fusion in stars. Some syllabi add tunnelling applications; keep WKB and resonant tunnelling out. Use a finite well only to show exponential tails.

figure.title: Tunnelling through a barrier
figure.aria: An incident wave hits a barrier, decays exponentially inside, exits with small amplitude, and gives transmission approximately e to the minus two kappa a.

chapters.example: An electron of energy E = 1.0 eV faces a rectangular barrier of height V = 2.0 eV and width a = 0.5 nm. Estimate the transmission probability using T ≈ e^(−2κa), with κ = √(2m(V−E))/ℏ. Use ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg and 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Answer: κ = 5.12 × 10⁹ m⁻¹; 2κa = 5.12; T ≈ 6.0 × 10⁻³ = 0.60%.
chapters.trap: Using T ≈ e^(−2κa) outside the thick-barrier limit. Also remember tunnelling needs E < V and a finite barrier width.
chapters.prereq: 6.8 particle in a box; 6.7 time-independent equation; exponential decay.
chapters.leave: WKB approximation, resonant tunnelling and Josephson effects; advanced quantum texts.
